## Problem

Three tests skip themselves when `ssh-keygen` is not on PATH, and one also skips
when `go` is missing. The CI job depends on the runner image providing
`ssh-keygen`; that dependency is recorded in a comment and enforced by nothing.
If the binary ever stops being present, every SSH-key path stops being tested
and the suite still reports `ok`.

## Evidence

The skips:

```go
// a_test.go:150
if _, lookErr := exec.LookPath("ssh-keygen"); lookErr != nil {
    t.Skip("ssh-keygen not available")
}

// a_test.go:296 (TestCLIIntegration)
if _, err := exec.LookPath(bin); err != nil {
    t.Skipf("%s not available", bin)
}

// internal/cmd/decrypt_test.go:134
if _, err := exec.LookPath("ssh-keygen"); err != nil {
    t.Skip("ssh-keygen not available")
}
```

The dependency, asserted only in prose:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/test.yml:17
runs-on: ubuntu-latest # ships ssh-keygen, which the key-generating tests need
```

What goes untested if the skip fires. `decrypt_test.go`'s helper at :134 feeds
`TestTryDecrypt_PassphraseProtectedKeyRoundTrip`, `TestTryDecrypt_WrongPassphrase`,
`TestTryDecrypt_PassphraseProtectedKeyIsDiagnosed`,
`TestDecryptCmd_SurfacesPassphraseDiagnosis` and
`TestDecryptCmd_ScanPathRoundTrip` — the entire passphrase-protected-key
feature, which commit 28f8e35 added precisely because it was broken. `a_test.go`
:296 gates `TestCLIIntegration`, which docs/audit/analysis-notes.md names as the
only thing covering `main()` at all.

Go reports a skipped test as a pass at the package level: `go test ./...` prints
`ok` either way, and the workflow has no step that would notice the coverage
drop.

## Impact

The suite's most load-bearing tests are the ones that can vanish without a red
check. A runner image change, a container-based runner, or anyone running
`go test ./...` in a minimal environment gets a green result that means "the SSH
paths were not exercised" — which is indistinguishable, from the outside, from
"the SSH paths work".

This is the same silence-reads-as-approval pattern the repo already fixed for
checkov, whose hook "silently never ran — 'Skipped', which reads like 'Passed'"
(.pre-commit-config.yaml:79-84).

## Fix

Make the skip conditional on not being in CI, so it stays a convenience locally
and becomes a failure where the dependency is promised. Add a helper in each
package and use it at the three sites:

```go
// requireSSHKeygen skips locally when ssh-keygen is absent, but fails in CI:
// the runner image is expected to ship it, and a silent skip there hides the
// loss of every passphrase-protected-key and key-scan test behind a green run.
func requireSSHKeygen(t *testing.T) {
    t.Helper()
    if _, err := exec.LookPath("ssh-keygen"); err != nil {
        if os.Getenv("CI") != "" {
            t.Fatalf("ssh-keygen missing on a CI runner that must provide it: %v", err)
        }
        t.Skip("ssh-keygen not available")
    }
}
```

GitHub Actions sets `CI=true` on every runner, so no workflow change is needed
for this half.

Cheaper alternative, or in addition — assert it once in the workflow, before
`go test`:

```yaml
- name: Assert the runner provides ssh-keygen
  # The key-generating tests skip without it, and a skip reads as a pass.
  run: command -v ssh-keygen
```

## Resolution
Both halves. In-test: internal/cmd's existing requireSSHKeygen and a new requireBinary in a_test.go now call t.Fatalf when the binary is absent and CI is set, and t.Skip otherwise; the two ad-hoc LookPath skips in a_test.go (generateSSHKeyPair, TestCLIIntegration) now route through requireBinary. In-workflow: test.yml gained an "Assert the runner provides ssh-keygen" step before `go test`. Verified the branch actually fires — running with CI=true and ssh-keygen off PATH fails with "ssh-keygen missing on a CI runner that must provide it" where it previously reported ok. Normal runs, with and without CI=true, still pass.
title: CI's ssh-keygen dependency is unasserted, so losing it would void the SSH tests silently

## Problem

`setupLogging` opens `cfg.LogFilePath` with `O_APPEND` and never rotates,
truncates, or caps it. Every invocation writes at least one record naming the
input path, the output path, the recipient list and the GitHub user. Nothing in
the tool, the packages, or the documentation bounds the file's growth or its
retention.

## Evidence

a.go:99

```go
logFile, err := os.OpenFile(cfg.LogFilePath, os.O_CREATE|os.O_WRONLY|os.O_APPEND, 0o600)
```

What each run appends — internal/cmd/encrypt.go:123-127:

```go
log.Info("Encrypting file",
    "input", input,
    "output", output,
    "recipients", allRecipients,
    "githubUser", ghUser)
```

and internal/cmd/decrypt.go:159:

```go
log.Info("Trying decryption with SSH key", "input", input, "output", output, "sshKey", keyPath)
```

The default location is `$XDG_STATE_HOME/a/cli.log`, created by
`applyConfigDefaults` (internal/cmd/config_shared.go:142-158). No `logrotate`
fragment ships in `.goreleaser.yml`'s `nfpms.contents`, which installs only the
three documentation files. The README's Configuration table documents
`log_file_path` as "JSON log file" with no mention that it is append-only and
unmanaged.

Every other retention knob in the tool is configurable and documented:
`cache_ttl_minutes` bounds the key cache, and the cache directory is named in
the README. Log retention is the one that is neither.

## Impact

Two consequences, both slow:

The file is unbounded. A scripted or heavy user accumulates a log that nothing
ever reclaims, in `~/.local/state`, where nobody looks.

More to the point for this tool: the log is a permanent, cleartext index of
every file the user encrypted and decrypted — filenames, destinations,
recipients and correspondents' GitHub usernames — kept forever by default, by a
program whose entire purpose is confidentiality. The ciphertext protects the
contents; the log narrates the metadata beside it. `0600` limits that to the
local account, which is the right permission and not a substitute for a
retention answer. A user who encrypts a file, wipes the plaintext and moves on
has left the filename behind indefinitely without being told.

## Fix

Smallest change that closes the unbounded case — cap the file at open, in
a.go's `setupLogging`:

```go
// Roll the log at 5 MiB. slog appends forever otherwise, and this file is a
// cleartext index of every path the user encrypted: unbounded growth is also
// unbounded retention.
const maxLogBytes = 5 << 20
if info, statErr := os.Stat(cfg.LogFilePath); statErr == nil && info.Size() > maxLogBytes {
    _ = os.Rename(cfg.LogFilePath, cfg.LogFilePath+".1")
}
```

One previous generation is kept, so a rotation cannot destroy the record of the
run that triggered it.

Then say so in the README's Configuration table, so the retention is a choice
the user can make rather than a default they never saw:

```markdown
| `log_file_path` | JSON log of every encrypt/decrypt, including file paths and recipients. Defaults to `$XDG_STATE_HOME/a/cli.log` (`~/.local/state/a/cli.log`), mode `0600`, rolled to `cli.log.1` past 5 MiB. Point it at `/dev/null` to keep no record. |
```

Verify `a` still logs after the roll and that `cli.log.1` appears once the cap
is crossed.

## Resolution
Added rollLog in a.go, called from setupLogging before the file is opened: past maxLogBytes (5 MiB) the log is renamed to <path>.1, keeping one previous generation so a roll cannot destroy the record of the run that triggered it. Every failure is ignored deliberately, matching setupLogging's existing stance that logging must not brick a command; the docstring says so. README's log_file_path row now describes what the file records, its mode, the roll threshold, and how to keep no record at all.
title: The JSON log grows without bound and records every file path encrypted or decrypted

## Problem

Three gaps between the README and the shipped CLI. One flag exists and is
undocumented; one config key's default is never stated, although `rem` restores
it; and the description of what disables caching is narrower than the code.

## Evidence

**1. `--github-user` appears nowhere in the README.** The flag exists:

```text
$ a encrypt --help
      --github-user string   GitHub username to fetch public keys for encryption
```

The README documents the positional form only — `encrypt [input] [github-user]`
in the Commands table (README.md:89) — and its list of long flags at :94-95
covers `-i`, `-o`, `-r` and `--ssh-key` but not this one. The positional and the
flag are not interchangeable in every position: with `--input` set, the
positional slot shifts (internal/cmd/encrypt.go:101-108), which is precisely
when a reader would reach for the flag and not find it.

**2. The default `cache_ttl_minutes` is never stated.** README.md:135 says only:

```markdown
| `cache_ttl_minutes` | Lifetime of cached GitHub keys; `0` disables caching |
```

The default is 120, written into every freshly bootstrapped config
(internal/cmd/config_shared.go:16, :67) and restored by
`a config rem cache_ttl_minutes` (internal/cmd/config.go:117). README.md:120
tells the user `rem` "resets one key" without saying to what, so the one
documented way to find the default is to run the command and read the output.

**3. "`0` disables caching" understates the condition.** The code disables
caching for any non-positive value:

```go
// internal/cmd/encrypt.go:209
if cfg.CacheDir != "" && cfg.CacheTTLMinutes > 0 {
```

`a config set cache_ttl_minutes -5` is accepted (`strconv.Atoi` takes it) and
also disables caching, which the table does not say.

## Impact

Individually minor; together they land on the same key. A user debugging a stale
GitHub key — the failure filed as audit-a6e37452 — goes to the README for the
cache controls, and finds a table that does not say what the TTL currently is,
what `rem` would set it to, or that the cache lives at a path they may need to
clear. The flag gap costs less, but `--github-user` is the only documented
public behaviour with no documentation.

## Fix

Add the flag to the long-form list at README.md:94-95:

```markdown
Add `-v` for verbose (debug) logging, and `--version` to print the build version
(quote it in bug reports). The long flag form still works:
`encrypt -i in -o out -r key.pub --github-user octocat`,
`decrypt -i in -o out --ssh-key key`.
```

Restate the cache row at README.md:135:

```markdown
| `cache_ttl_minutes` | Lifetime of cached GitHub keys, in minutes. Default `120`; `a config rem cache_ttl_minutes` restores it. Zero or negative disables caching entirely |
```

And name the cache path as the thing to clear, in the paragraph at :138-140
that already gives it:

```markdown
Fetched GitHub keys are cached (mode `0600`) in the user cache dir
(`~/.cache/a/<user>.keys` on Linux, `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/a/` if set) for
`cache_ttl_minutes`, avoiding a network request on every encryption. Delete the
file to force a refresh before the TTL expires.
```

## Resolution
All three gaps closed in README.md: --github-user added to the long-flag example line; the cache_ttl_minutes row now gives the default (120), says `rem` restores it, and states that zero or negative disables caching, not just zero; the cache paragraph names $XDG_CACHE_HOME and says to delete the file to force a refresh before the TTL. Also corrected "requires Go 1.25+" to 1.26+, which the x/crypto bump in audit-b87848dd made necessary. markdownlint clean.
title: README omits the --github-user flag and the cache_ttl_minutes default

## Problem

The `release` recipe invokes `goreleaser release --clean --skip-publish
--snapshot`. GoReleaser v2 removed the individual `--skip-*` flags in favour of
`--skip=<option>`, so the pinned 2.18.0 rejects the command outright. The recipe
is the only local dry run of the release pipeline, and it has never worked
against the pinned toolchain.

## Evidence

Justfile:41-43

```make
# Run GoReleaser (dry-run by default)
release:
    goreleaser release --clean --skip-publish --snapshot
```

Against the version mise pins (2.18.0):

```text
$ goreleaser release --skip-publish --snapshot
  ⨯ command failed    error=unknown flag: --skip-publish

$ goreleaser release --help | grep -- --skip
    --skip   Skip the given options (valid options are announce, archive, aur,
             ..., publish, sbom, scoop, sign, snapcraft, srpm, validate, winget)
```

The flag is also redundant. `--help` documents `--snapshot` as: "Generate an
unversioned snapshot release, skipping all validations and without publishing
any artifacts (implies --skip=announce,publish,validate)".

## Impact

There is no working local rehearsal of the release. Every change to
`.goreleaser.yml` — the archive file list, the nfpm contents, the cosign `signs`
block, the `dockers_v2` build — is exercised for the first time by release.yml,
which only fires on a pushed `v*.*.*` tag. A config error there fails a job that
already holds `contents: write` and `packages: write`, after the tag exists in
the repository, so recovery means deleting and re-pushing a tag rather than
fixing a red check on a PR.

mise.toml pins cosign and syft specifically so that "a local release run"
exercises what CI does; that stated purpose is unreachable while the recipe
cannot start.

## Fix

Drop the removed flag — `--snapshot` already implies it:

```make
# Run GoReleaser (dry-run by default)
release:
    goreleaser release --clean --snapshot
```

Verify with `just release`, which should now reach the build stage and produce
`dist/`. If the intent was a dry run that still validates (no snapshot
versioning), use `goreleaser release --clean --skip=publish,announce` instead.

## Resolution
Dropped --skip-publish; the recipe is now `goreleaser release --clean --snapshot`, and --snapshot already implies --skip=announce,publish,validate. Verified end to end: `just release` previously died on "unknown flag: --skip-publish" and now reaches "building snapshot... version=1.0.1-next" and compiles every target (linux_arm64_v8.0, freebsd_amd64_v1, linux_arm_7, linux_arm_6, linux_386_sse2, darwin_arm64_v8.0, ...). The local release rehearsal works for the first time. Moved the rationale above a [doc("Run GoReleaser (dry-run by default)")] attribute — `just --list` shows only the comment line adjacent to the recipe, so the multi-line explanation had hijacked the description; same treatment applied to precommit and the new vuln recipe.
title: `just release` passes --skip-publish, a flag GoReleaser v2 does not have

## Problem

Defect class: coverage-hole, confirmed mutation-blind. `Encrypt`'s RunE converts
an `encryptFile` failure into a command error. No test in the suite ever makes
`encryptFile` fail *through the command* — every test that reaches RunE either
supplies a working recipient set and a writable output, or fails earlier in
validation. The branch that turns a failed encryption into a nonzero exit is
therefore unguarded.

## Evidence

The unguarded branch — internal/cmd/encrypt.go:129-135:

```go
			if err := encryptFile(input, output, recips); err != nil {
				log.Error("Encryption failed", "error", err)
				return fmt.Errorf("encryption failed: %w", err)
			}

			log.Info("Encryption successful")
			return nil
```

`encryptFile`'s own failures *are* tested, but only by calling it directly, never
through the command — internal/cmd/encrypt_test.go:256-259 and :264-271:

```go
func TestEncryptFile_MissingInput(t *testing.T) {
	err := encryptFile("/no/such/input", filepath.Join(t.TempDir(), "o.age"), nil)
	assert.ErrorContains(t, err, "opening input")
}
```

The two tests that do drive RunE to an error stop before `encryptFile` is
reached: `TestEncryptCmd_BuildArgsError` fails in `parseRecipients` ("empty
recipient"), and `TestEncryptCmd_AgeFailure` — despite its name — also fails in
`parseRecipients`, because `age1bogusrecipient` is neither a readable file nor a
parseable key, so `age` is never invoked:

```go
// internal/cmd/errpaths_test.go:101-109
func TestEncryptCmd_AgeFailure(t *testing.T) {
	...
	c := Encrypt(&Config{DefaultRecipients: []string{"age1bogusrecipient"}}, discardLogger())
	...
	assert.Error(t, c.RunE(c, nil))
}
```

Mutation spot-check, run against a scratch copy of the tree:

```text
--- M1: Encrypt RunE drops the encryptFile error check ---
    if err := encryptFile(input, output, recips); err != nil {
        log.Error("Encryption failed", "error", err)
        return fmt.Errorf("encryption failed: %w", err)
    }
  becomes
    _ = encryptFile(input, output, recips)

$ go test ./...
exit: 0   (MUTATION SURVIVED — whole suite still green)
```

Coverage confirms it independently: lines 131-133 report 0 executions, as do
every one of `encryptFile`'s own failure branches when reached from RunE
(360-361, 375-377, 380-382, 384-385, 387-388).

## Impact

With that branch mutated away, `a encrypt` prints "Encryption successful",
writes nothing, and exits 0 when encryption fails — a full-disk target, an
unwritable output directory, a recipient set age rejects at write time. This is
the data-loss shape the whole design guards against: the user sees success,
deletes the plaintext, and has nothing. The suite would not notice.

The same absence means the surrounding hardening is unverified too. Nothing
proves that a failed encryption leaves no partial `.age` at the target path when
the failure arrives through the command rather than through a direct call.

## Fix

Add a test that reaches `encryptFile` with a valid recipient and a target it
cannot write, to `internal/cmd/fetch_test.go` beside the other RunE tests:

```go
// A failure inside encryptFile must surface as a command error. Dropping that
// branch makes `a encrypt` report success and exit 0 having written nothing --
// the user deletes the plaintext and has neither copy.
func TestEncryptCmd_EncryptFileFailureSurfaces(t *testing.T) {
	dir := t.TempDir()
	in := filepath.Join(dir, "msg.txt")
	require.NoError(t, os.WriteFile(in, []byte("plaintext"), 0o600))
	_, pub := makeSSHKey(t, dir)

	// Recipients parse, validation passes, and the output path is accepted --
	// but its directory is read-only, so encryptFile's CreateTemp fails.
	locked := filepath.Join(dir, "locked")
	require.NoError(t, os.Mkdir(locked, 0o500))
	t.Cleanup(func() { _ = os.Chmod(locked, 0o700) })

	c := Encrypt(&Config{DefaultRecipients: []string{pub}}, discardLogger())
	require.NoError(t, c.Flags().Set("input", in))
	require.NoError(t, c.Flags().Set("output", filepath.Join(locked, "out.age")))

	err := c.RunE(c, nil)
	require.Error(t, err, "a failed encryption must not exit 0")
	assert.ErrorContains(t, err, "encryption failed")
	assert.NoFileExists(t, filepath.Join(locked, "out.age"))
}
```

Prove failing-capability by re-running M1 with the test in place: the suite must
now fail.

Separately, rename `TestEncryptCmd_AgeFailure` to `TestEncryptCmd_BadRecipientFailure`
— it never reaches age, and its current name is what made this hole look covered.

## Resolution
Added TestEncryptCmd_EncryptFileFailureSurfaces (internal/cmd/fetch_test.go): valid recipient, validation passes, output directory 0500 so encryptFile's CreateTemp fails. Asserts the command errors with "encryption failed" and leaves nothing at the output path. Also renamed TestEncryptCmd_AgeFailure to TestEncryptCmd_BadRecipientFailure and gave it an ErrorContains on "invalid recipient" — the old name is what made this hole look covered, since it never reaches age. Failing-capability proof: mutation M1 (replace the encryptFile error check with `_ = encryptFile(...)`) went from exit 0 (suite green) before to exit 1 after. encryptFile also rose 74.1% to 88.9% via TestEncryptFile_WriteFailures, which covers CreateTemp, io.Copy and Rename failures directly.
title: No test makes encryptFile fail through the command, so exiting 0 on a failed encryption ships silently

## Problem

Defect class: coverage-hole, confirmed mutation-blind. `Decrypt`'s RunE calls
`ensureWritableOutput` before attempting any key. `encrypt` has a full test for
the equivalent guard; `decrypt` has none. The asymmetry is the tell: the same
protection exists on both commands, and only one of them is pinned.

## Evidence

The unguarded wiring — internal/cmd/decrypt.go:203-206:

```go
			force, _ := cmd.Flags().GetBool("force")
			if err := ensureWritableOutput(output, force); err != nil {
				return err
			}
```

`ensureWritableOutput` itself is tested as a unit
(internal/cmd/fetch_test.go:154-165), and encrypt's use of it is tested through
the command (`TestEncryptCmd_RefusesExistingOutput`, fetch_test.go:169-197,
which asserts the pre-existing bytes survive and that `--force` replaces them).
There is no `TestDecryptCmd_RefusesExistingOutput`. Every decrypt-command test
writes to a fresh path:

```go
// decrypt_test.go:259  TestDecryptCmd_SurfacesPassphraseDiagnosis
require.NoError(t, c.Flags().Set("output", filepath.Join(dir, "m.dec")))
// decrypt_test.go:307  TestDecryptCmd_ScanPathRoundTrip
dec := filepath.Join(home, "dec.txt")
```

Mutation spot-check, run against a scratch copy of the tree:

```text
--- M2: Decrypt RunE drops the ensureWritableOutput guard ---
    force, _ := cmd.Flags().GetBool("force")
    if err := ensureWritableOutput(output, force); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    sshKeyFlag, _ := cmd.Flags().GetString("ssh-key")
  becomes
    sshKeyFlag, _ := cmd.Flags().GetString("ssh-key")

$ go test ./...
exit: 0   (MUTATION SURVIVED — whole suite still green)
```

Coverage agrees: decrypt.go:205-206 reports 0 executions.

## Impact

`decrypt` derives its output path by default — `secret.txt.age` becomes
`secret.txt` — so the destructive case is the ordinary one: the user names one
file and the tool picks a target that frequently already exists. With the guard
mutated away, `a d notes.txt.age` overwrites a `notes.txt` the user has since
edited, reverting it to the older decrypted content, silently and with exit 0.
`tryDecrypt` finishes with `os.Rename`, which replaces the destination
unconditionally, so there is no second line of defence.

The commit that added this guard (28f8e35) names exactly that scenario as the
reason it exists. Nothing currently stops it being removed again.

## Fix

Mirror the encrypt test. Add to `internal/cmd/decrypt_test.go`:

```go
// The mirror of TestEncryptCmd_RefusesExistingOutput. decrypt derives its
// output path, so the destructive case is the common one: `a d notes.txt.age`
// targets a notes.txt the user may have edited since. Rename replaces
// unconditionally, so this guard is the only thing standing in front of it.
func TestDecryptCmd_RefusesExistingOutput(t *testing.T) {
	dir := t.TempDir()
	priv, pub := makeSSHKey(t, dir)

	plain := filepath.Join(dir, "notes.txt")
	require.NoError(t, os.WriteFile(plain, []byte("original"), 0o600))
	enc := filepath.Join(dir, "notes.txt.age")
	recips, err := parseRecipients([]string{pub})
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.NoError(t, encryptFile(plain, enc, recips))

	// The user edits the plaintext after encrypting; decrypt must not revert it.
	require.NoError(t, os.WriteFile(plain, []byte("edited since"), 0o600))

	run := func(force bool) error {
		c := Decrypt(&Config{SSHKeyPath: priv}, discardLogger())
		require.NoError(t, c.Flags().Set("input", enc))
		if force {
			require.NoError(t, c.Flags().Set("force", "true"))
		}
		return c.RunE(c, nil) // output derives to notes.txt
	}

	err = run(false)
	require.Error(t, err, "decrypt must refuse to replace an existing output")
	assert.ErrorContains(t, err, "already exists")
	got, readErr := os.ReadFile(plain) // #nosec G304 -- test temp path
	require.NoError(t, readErr)
	assert.Equal(t, "edited since", string(got), "the newer plaintext must survive")

	require.NoError(t, run(true), "--force must permit replacement")
	got, readErr = os.ReadFile(plain) // #nosec G304 -- test temp path
	require.NoError(t, readErr)
	assert.Equal(t, "original", string(got), "--force restores the decrypted content")
}
```

Prove failing-capability by re-running M2 with the test in place: the suite must
now fail.

## Resolution
Added TestDecryptCmd_RefusesExistingOutput (internal/cmd/decrypt_test.go), mirroring TestEncryptCmd_RefusesExistingOutput: encrypt notes.txt, edit the plaintext, then decrypt with the derived output path. Asserts the run fails with "already exists", that the edited plaintext survives byte-for-byte, and that --force does replace it. Failing-capability proof: mutation M2 (delete the ensureWritableOutput call from Decrypt's RunE) went from exit 0 before to exit 1 after.
title: Nothing tests that decrypt refuses an existing output, so dropping the guard clobbers plaintext silently

body:
## Problem

Defect class: mutation-blind. `LoadConfig` refuses a config file with any bit set
in the group or other triplet. Exactly one test exercises it, with mode `0o644`
— which has bits in *both* triplets. A mutation that narrows the mask to only
group, or only other, still rejects `0o644`, so the suite cannot tell the two
halves apart and neither half is independently pinned.

## Evidence

The control — internal/cmd/config_shared.go:108-112:

```go
	if perm := info.Mode().Perm(); perm&0o077 != 0 {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf(
			"config file %s is group/other accessible (perms %#o); fix it with: chmod 600 %s",
			cfgFile, perm, cfgFile)
	}
```

The only test that drives it — internal/cmd/config_shared_test.go:42-51:

```go
func TestLoadConfig_RejectsGroupOtherPerms(t *testing.T) {
	p := filepath.Join(t.TempDir(), "config.yaml")
	// #nosec G306 -- intentionally lax perms to exercise the permission enforcement in LoadConfig
	require.NoError(t, os.WriteFile(p, []byte("github_user: x\n"), 0o644))
	_, err := LoadConfig(p)
	assert.ErrorContains(t, err, "group/other accessible")
	assert.ErrorContains(t, err, "chmod 600", "the error must name the fix")
}
```

`0o644` sets group `4` and other `4`. Any mask that keeps either triplet still
matches, so both narrowing mutations pass. Verified against a scratch copy:

```text
--- M6: perm&0o077 -> perm&0o007  (other-only; 0o640 would now be accepted) ---
$ go test ./...
exit: 0   (MUTATION SURVIVED)

--- M6b: perm&0o077 -> perm&0o070  (group-only; 0o604 would now be accepted) ---
$ go test ./...
exit: 0   (MUTATION SURVIVED)
```

The sibling test `TestLoadConfig_AcceptsStricterPerms` (config_shared_test.go:53)
pins the other direction with `0o400`, so the accept side is fine; it is the
reject side that has a single, undiscriminating case.

## Impact

Under M6, a config at `0o640` — the mode a restrictive `umask 027` produces, and
the common shape on a machine with a shared group — loads without complaint,
disclosing `ssh_key_path` and `github_user` to every member of that group. The
README states the opposite in as many words: "any bit set in the group or other
triplet — not just the read bits — makes `a` refuse to run and print the `chmod`
to apply." The suite would let that regression through.

Filed High rather than Critical deliberately: this is a documented security
control with an untested half, but the config file holds paths and a username,
not key material, so the disclosure is low-sensitivity. The gap is the untested
control, not a live compromise.

## Fix

Replace the single case with a table that separates the triplets, in
`internal/cmd/config_shared_test.go`:

```go
// Each mode isolates one triplet: 0640 has group bits only, 0604 other bits
// only, 0644 both. A single 0644 case cannot tell the halves apart, so
// narrowing the mask to 0o070 or 0o007 passed while silently accepting a
// group- or other-readable config.
func TestLoadConfig_RejectsGroupOtherPerms(t *testing.T) {
	for _, mode := range []os.FileMode{0o640, 0o604, 0o644, 0o610, 0o601} {
		t.Run(fmt.Sprintf("%#o", mode), func(t *testing.T) {
			p := filepath.Join(t.TempDir(), "config.yaml")
			require.NoError(t, os.WriteFile(p, []byte("github_user: x\n"), 0o600))
			// #nosec G302 -- intentionally lax perms to exercise the enforcement
			require.NoError(t, os.Chmod(p, mode))
			_, err := LoadConfig(p)
			require.Error(t, err, "%#o must be refused", mode)
			assert.ErrorContains(t, err, "group/other accessible")
			assert.ErrorContains(t, err, "chmod 600", "the error must name the fix")
		})
	}
}
```

`0o610` and `0o601` cover the execute bits, which the docstring calls out as
in-scope ("not just the read bits"). Write via `os.WriteFile` at `0600` then
`os.Chmod`, so the process umask cannot mask the bits under test.

Prove failing-capability by re-running M6 and M6b with the table in place: both
must now fail.

## Resolution
TestLoadConfig_RejectsGroupOtherPerms is now a subtest table over 0640, 0604, 0644, 0610 and 0601 — group-only, other-only, both, and the execute bits the check deliberately includes. Each writes at 0600 then chmods, so the process umask cannot clear the bits under test. Failing-capability proof: mutations M6 (mask narrowed to 0o007) and M6b (narrowed to 0o070) both went from exit 0 before to exit 1 after; previously a single 0644 case satisfied either narrowed mask.
title: The config permission check is tested with one 0644 case, so narrowing the mask to group-only or other-only survives

body:
## Problem

Defect class: assertion-free. `setupLogging` is called by three tests and
asserted on by none. Two of the call sites exist only to execute the function;
one states outright that its criterion is "must not panic". Nothing checks that
a log file is created, that anything is written to it, that the verbose flag
changes the level, or that the stderr fallback actually happens.

## Evidence

a_test.go:281-288 — the whole test:

```go
func TestSetupLoggingFallback(t *testing.T) {
	// Pointing the log path at a directory makes OpenFile fail; logging must
	// degrade to stderr rather than error, so a bad log_file_path cannot brick
	// every command (including the `config` command needed to fix it).
	dir := t.TempDir()
	cfg = &cmd.Config{LogFilePath: dir}
	setupLogging(false) // must not panic; degrades to stderr
}
```

a_test.go:78-79, the tail of `TestConfigWrappers`:

```go
	setupLogging(true)
	setupLogging(false)
```

Neither block contains an assertion. `TestSetupLoggingFallback` passes if
`setupLogging` returns without panicking — which it does for every possible
implementation, including an empty body, since the function returns nothing by
design. `TestConfigWrappers`' two trailing calls are pure line-coverage: they
mark `setupLogging` executed and verify nothing about the result.

The consequence is visible in what the suite failed to notice this session: a
`rollLog` call was added to `setupLogging` (a.go:99) and not one existing
assertion moved. Only the separately-written `TestRollLog` covers it, and that
test calls `rollLog` directly — nothing asserts that `setupLogging` invokes it.

## Impact

`setupLogging` owns the decision that a bad `log_file_path` must degrade to
stderr rather than error, which is what keeps a broken config from bricking
every command including the `config` command needed to repair it. That
behaviour is load-bearing and entirely unpinned: an edit that made the failure
fatal, or that silently stopped opening the log at all, passes the suite.

The docstring makes the stakes explicit — "It returns nothing on purpose. An
error return here is a slot a later edit can fill with `return err`,
reintroducing exactly that bricking" — and then no test enforces it.

## Fix

Give both call sites real assertions. Replace a_test.go:281-288 with:

```go
func TestSetupLoggingFallback(t *testing.T) {
	// Pointing the log path at a directory makes OpenFile fail; logging must
	// degrade to stderr rather than error, so a bad log_file_path cannot brick
	// every command (including the `config` command needed to fix it).
	dir := t.TempDir()
	cfg = &cmd.Config{LogFilePath: dir}

	setupLogging(false)

	// The fallback logger must be usable and must not have created anything at
	// the bad path. "Must not panic" was the old criterion and an empty body
	// satisfied it.
	log.Info("probe")
	entries, err := os.ReadDir(dir)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	assert.Empty(t, entries, "the directory log path must not gain a file")
}
```

And replace the two bare calls in `TestConfigWrappers` (a_test.go:78-79) with a
check that the configured file is actually opened, written, and levelled:

```go
	setupLogging(true) // verbose -> debug level
	log.Debug("debug probe")
	body, err := os.ReadFile(cfg.LogFilePath) // #nosec G304 -- test temp path
	require.NoError(t, err, "setupLogging must open the configured log file")
	assert.Contains(t, string(body), "debug probe", "verbose must admit Debug records")

	setupLogging(false) // non-verbose -> Debug is filtered out
	log.Debug("must not appear")
	body, err = os.ReadFile(cfg.LogFilePath) // #nosec G304 -- test temp path
	require.NoError(t, err)
	assert.NotContains(t, string(body), "must not appear", "non-verbose must filter Debug")
```

Prove failing-capability by emptying `setupLogging`'s body in a scratch copy:
the suite must fail, where today it passes.

## Resolution
Both call sites now assert. TestSetupLoggingFallback logs through the fallback logger and asserts the directory log path gained no file. TestConfigWrappers' two bare calls became a verbose/non-verbose pair: setupLogging(true) then log.Debug must appear in the configured file, setupLogging(false) then a second Debug must not — which pins that the file is opened, written, and levelled. Failing-capability proof: mutation M12 (drop the rollLog call and point OpenFile at os.DevNull) went from exit 0 before to exit 1 after.
title: Both setupLogging tests are assertion-free; the function could do nothing and stay green

body:
## Problem

Defect class: mutation-blind. The test exists to pin `tryDecrypt`'s empty-path
guard, but asserts only that an error occurred. Every one of its three cases
also errors for an unrelated reason once the guard is gone — `os.ReadFile` fails
on the empty or bogus key path — so deleting the guard entirely leaves the test
green.

## Evidence

The guard — internal/cmd/decrypt.go:86-88:

```go
	if keyPath == "" || output == "" || input == "" {
		return fmt.Errorf("invalid arguments for decryption: empty path")
	}
```

The test — internal/cmd/decrypt_test.go:55-59:

```go
func TestTryDecrypt_EmptyPath(t *testing.T) {
	assert.Error(t, tryDecrypt("", "o.txt", "i"))
	assert.Error(t, tryDecrypt("k", "", "i"))
	assert.Error(t, tryDecrypt("k", "o.txt", ""))
}
```

Without the guard, control reaches `os.ReadFile(keyPath)` in all three cases:
`ReadFile("")` fails, and `ReadFile("k")` fails because no such file exists in
the test's working directory. Three errors, three passing assertions, wrong
reason in every case.

Mutation spot-check against a scratch copy:

```text
--- M3: tryDecrypt drops the empty-path guard ---
$ go test ./...
exit: 0   (MUTATION SURVIVED)
```

## Impact

Low: the guard is defensive, and the callers that matter — `Decrypt`'s RunE and
`tryAllKeys` — reject empty paths earlier through `resolveIO` and the key-scan
branch. The cost is a test that reads as protection and is not: someone
refactoring `tryDecrypt` deletes the guard, sees green, and ships a function
whose contract has quietly changed from "rejects empty paths" to "fails
somewhere downstream with a confusing message about a file named ''".

## Fix

Assert the message, so the error has to come from the guard and not from the
filesystem:

```go
func TestTryDecrypt_EmptyPath(t *testing.T) {
	// ErrorContains, not Error: with the guard deleted all three still fail --
	// on os.ReadFile -- so a bare Error assertion pins nothing.
	const want = "empty path"
	assert.ErrorContains(t, tryDecrypt("", "o.txt", "i"), want, "empty key path")
	assert.ErrorContains(t, tryDecrypt("k", "", "i"), want, "empty output path")
	assert.ErrorContains(t, tryDecrypt("k", "o.txt", ""), want, "empty input path")
}
```

Prove failing-capability by re-running M3 with the change in place: the suite
must now fail.

## Resolution
TestTryDecrypt_EmptyPath now uses ErrorContains on "empty path" for all three cases instead of bare assert.Error. Failing-capability proof: mutation M3 (delete the empty-path guard from tryDecrypt) went from exit 0 before to exit 1 after — previously all three still errored via os.ReadFile, so the test passed against a tryDecrypt with no guard at all.
title: TestTryDecrypt_EmptyPath passes with the guard it targets deleted

body:
## Problem

Defect class: weak assertion, at class scale. Ten assertions across four test
files check only that *an* error occurred, never which one. On the error paths
they guard, several distinct failures are reachable from the same call, so the
tests cannot tell the intended failure from an unrelated one — and the error
text, which for this tool is the entire user-facing remedy, is unpinned.

## Evidence

The sites:

```text
internal/cmd/errpaths_test.go:40   TestInitConfigPaths_ConfigMkdirError
internal/cmd/errpaths_test.go:49   TestInitConfigPaths_CacheMkdirError
internal/cmd/errpaths_test.go:62   TestLoadConfig_DefaultsError
internal/cmd/errpaths_test.go:67   TestApplyConfigDefaults_MkdirError
internal/cmd/errpaths_test.go:75   TestLoadConfig_MissingDefaultsError
internal/cmd/errpaths_test.go:90   TestInitConfigPaths_UserConfigDirError
internal/cmd/errpaths_test.go:98   TestLoadConfig_ReadError
internal/cmd/config_shared_test.go:74   TestSaveConfig_Error
internal/cmd/config_shared_test.go:109  TestScanSSHPrivateKeys (missing ~/.ssh)
a_test.go:317                      TestInitConfigPathsWrapperError
```

Representative pair — internal/cmd/errpaths_test.go:35-50:

```go
func TestInitConfigPaths_ConfigMkdirError(t *testing.T) {
	t.Setenv("HOME", t.TempDir())
	t.Setenv("XDG_CONFIG_HOME", blockedPath(t))
	t.Setenv("XDG_CACHE_HOME", filepath.Join(t.TempDir(), "cache"))
	_, err := InitConfigPaths()
	assert.Error(t, err)
}

func TestInitConfigPaths_CacheMkdirError(t *testing.T) {
	home := t.TempDir()
	t.Setenv("HOME", home)
	t.Setenv("XDG_CONFIG_HOME", filepath.Join(home, "cfg"))
	t.Setenv("XDG_CACHE_HOME", blockedPath(t))
	_, err := InitConfigPaths()
	assert.Error(t, err)
}
```

`InitConfigPaths` has five distinct error returns. Neither test proves which one
fired, so the two are interchangeable: swap the config and cache branches in
production and both still pass.

Mutation spot-check confirming the class is real, run against a scratch copy —
`SaveConfig`'s `CreateTemp` error return replaced with an unrelated message:

```text
--- M9: SaveConfig CreateTemp error -> fmt.Errorf("totally unrelated message") ---
$ go test ./...
exit: 0   (MUTATION SURVIVED)
```

The suite already knows the stronger pattern and applies it elsewhere:
`TestLoadConfig_StatError` uses `assert.ErrorContains(t, err, "could not stat")`,
and `TestLoadConfig_RejectsGroupOtherPerms` asserts the message names `chmod 600`
with the comment "the error must name the fix". The ten above are the sites that
did not get it.

## Impact

Error text is this tool's remedy channel — several messages exist specifically to
tell the user what to run next, and the repo treats that as a requirement, not a
nicety. A refactor that collapses two branches, drops the `%w` wrapping, or
replaces a specific message with a generic one keeps all ten green. The tests
record that something failed, which is the part that was never in doubt.

## Fix

Replace each `assert.Error(t, err)` with `assert.ErrorContains` naming the
message that path must produce. The five with distinct existing text:

```go
// errpaths_test.go:40
assert.ErrorContains(t, err, "not a directory")           // config MkdirAll
// errpaths_test.go:49
assert.ErrorContains(t, err, "not a directory")           // cache MkdirAll
// errpaths_test.go:62 and :75
assert.ErrorContains(t, err, "resolving home directory for the default log path")
// errpaths_test.go:67
assert.ErrorContains(t, err, "resolving home directory for the default log path")
// config_shared_test.go:109
assert.ErrorContains(t, err, ".ssh")                      // ScanSSHPrivateKeys
```

The two `InitConfigPaths` MkdirAll cases still share a message, so distinguish
them by the path in the error instead:

```go
// errpaths_test.go:40
assert.ErrorContains(t, err, cfgBlocked, "the failure must name the config path")
// errpaths_test.go:49
assert.ErrorContains(t, err, cacheBlocked, "the failure must name the cache path")
```

capturing `blockedPath(t)`'s return in a variable so it can be asserted on.

Prove failing-capability by re-running M9 with the changes in place, and by
swapping the config and cache error branches in a scratch copy: both must now
fail.

## Resolution
All ten bare assert.Error calls now assert the message. Correction to the finding: its suggested text for the three fileHome-based tests was wrong. fileHome points HOME at a regular file, so os.UserHomeDir succeeds and it is the subsequent MkdirAll that fails — the error is "not a directory", not "resolving home directory for the default log path". I probed each path for its actual message before asserting rather than trusting the finding. Final assertions: "not a directory" for the four MkdirAll paths (the two InitConfigPaths cases additionally assert filepath.Dir(blockedPath) so they are not interchangeable), "neither $XDG_CONFIG_HOME nor $HOME are defined", "is a directory", "no such file or directory", ".ssh", "yaml:", and `invalid recipient "garbage-not-a-key"`. ## Problem

Defect class: weak assertion, confirmed mutation-blind. The test runs all three
shells and asserts each returns no error. All three generators return nil for
any shell, so the assertion cannot distinguish them: the switch could map every
case to the same generator and the test would still pass.

## Evidence

internal/cmd/completion_test.go:27-34 — the whole test:

```go
func TestCompletion_ValidShells(t *testing.T) {
	root := &cobra.Command{Use: "a"}
	c := Completion(root)
	for _, shell := range []string{"bash", "zsh", "fish"} {
		err := withSuppressedStdout(t, func() error { return c.RunE(c, []string{shell}) })
		assert.NoError(t, err, "shell %s should generate completion", shell)
	}
}
```

`withSuppressedStdout` redirects `os.Stdout` to a temp file and discards it, so
the generated script is never inspected — only the error value is.

Mutation spot-check against a scratch copy:

```text
--- M7: Completion maps "bash" to GenZshCompletion ---
    case "bash":
        return rootCmd.GenBashCompletion(os.Stdout)
  becomes
    case "bash":
        return rootCmd.GenZshCompletion(os.Stdout)

$ go test ./...
exit: 0   (MUTATION SURVIVED)
```

## Impact

Advisory: the failure mode is a user sourcing the wrong script and getting no
completions, which is visible and harmless. But the test is the only thing
standing behind the dispatch, and the exact output is trivially checkable — the
generated scripts carry distinguishing markers — so the weak assertion buys
nothing.

Note that `withSuppressedStdout` already writes the script to a temp file. The
content is captured and then thrown away; asserting on it costs one read.

## Fix

Have the helper return what was written, and assert a shell-specific marker:

```go
// withCapturedStdout redirects os.Stdout while fn runs and returns what it
// wrote. Capturing rather than discarding is what lets the caller assert which
// shell's script was produced: every generator returns nil, so an error-only
// assertion cannot tell GenBashCompletion from GenZshCompletion.
func withCapturedStdout(t *testing.T, fn func() error) (string, error) {
	t.Helper()
	old := os.Stdout
	f, err := os.CreateTemp(t.TempDir(), "stdout")
	require.NoError(t, err)
	os.Stdout = f
	runErr := fn()
	os.Stdout = old
	require.NoError(t, f.Close())
	out, err := os.ReadFile(f.Name()) // #nosec G304 -- test temp path
	require.NoError(t, err)
	return string(out), runErr
}

func TestCompletion_ValidShells(t *testing.T) {
	root := &cobra.Command{Use: "a"}
	c := Completion(root)
	// Markers unique to each generator's output, so mapping a case to the wrong
	// generator fails instead of passing on a nil error.
	for shell, marker := range map[string]string{
		"bash": "__start_a",
		"zsh":  "#compdef",
		"fish": "__fish_a_",
	} {
		out, err := withCapturedStdout(t, func() error { return c.RunE(c, []string{shell}) })
		require.NoError(t, err, "shell %s should generate completion", shell)
		assert.Contains(t, out, marker, "%s must produce the %s script", shell, shell)
	}
}
```

Confirm the three markers against the installed cobra version before committing
— they come from its generator templates, not from this repo. Prove
failing-capability by re-running M7: the suite must now fail.

## Resolution
withSuppressedStdout became withCapturedStdout, returning what the generator wrote, and TestCompletion_ValidShells asserts a per-shell marker. Correction to the finding: its suggested fish marker "__fish_a_" does not appear in cobra's fish script — the first attempt failed on it. I then enumerated candidate markers against all three generated scripts and picked ones confirmed to appear in exactly one: "__start_a" (bash), "#compdef" (zsh), "# fish completion for a" (fish). Failing-capability proof: mutation M7 (map bash to GenZshCompletion) went from exit 0 before to exit 1 after.
title: TestCompletion_ValidShells asserts only NoError, so bash generating a zsh script passes

## Problem

Defect class: tautological. The test's second assertion checks that
`buildVersion()` returns something non-empty when no ldflags stamp is set. Every
return path of `buildVersion` yields a non-empty string by construction, so the
assertion holds for any implementation — including ones that return the wrong
value. The exact value is known and checkable.

## Evidence

a_test.go:28-37:

```go
func TestBuildVersionPrefersLdflagsStamp(t *testing.T) {
	old := version
	t.Cleanup(func() { version = old })

	version = "1.2.3-stamped"
	assert.Equal(t, "1.2.3-stamped", buildVersion(), "an ldflags stamp must win")

	version = ""
	assert.NotEmpty(t, buildVersion(), "with no stamp, fall back to build info")
}
```

The function — a.go:34-42:

```go
func buildVersion() string {
	if version != "" {
		return version
	}
	if info, ok := debug.ReadBuildInfo(); ok && info.Main.Version != "" && info.Main.Version != "(devel)" {
		return info.Main.Version
	}
	return "(devel)"
}
```

Path 1 is guarded by `version != ""`, path 2 by `info.Main.Version != ""`, and
path 3 is the constant `"(devel)"`. No path can return an empty string, so
`assert.NotEmpty` is a statement about the type, not about the behaviour.

The value under test is not merely non-empty but fixed and knowable. Probed
directly:

```text
$ go test -run TestBVProbe -v .
    bv_test.go:8: buildVersion() under go test = "(devel)"
--- PASS
```

The first assertion is fine and is what the test's name is about; only the
fallback line is inert.

## Impact

Advisory. The stamp-wins behaviour — the part that actually broke once and
motivated the test — is properly pinned by the first assertion. The second line
adds the appearance of fallback coverage without any. A change to the fallback
constant, or one that removed the `!= "(devel)"` guard, would pass.

## Fix

Assert the value the function is documented to produce:

```go
	version = ""
	// "(devel)" exactly, not merely non-empty: every return path of
	// buildVersion is non-empty by construction, so NotEmpty asserts the type
	// rather than the behaviour. Under `go test` ReadBuildInfo reports
	// Main.Version as "(devel)", which the guard rejects, so the constant is
	// what must come back.
	assert.Equal(t, "(devel)", buildVersion(),
		"with no stamp and no release build info, the honest answer is (devel)")
```

Prove failing-capability by changing the fallback constant to `"unknown"` in a
scratch copy: the test must fail, where today it passes.

## Resolution
The fallback assertion is now assert.Equal on "(devel)" rather than assert.NotEmpty, with a comment recording that every return path of buildVersion is non-empty by construction so NotEmpty asserted the type rather than the behavior. The expected value was probed under go test before asserting it. Failing-capability proof: mutation M13 (fallback constant changed to "unknown") went from exit 0 before to exit 1 after.
title: TestBuildVersionPrefersLdflagsStamp's NotEmpty fallback assertion cannot fail

## Problem

The run was asked to take coverage to 100%. It cannot get there under the
constraint this command works within — test files only, production source never
modified — and it is worth recording why, so the next person does not spend the
effort discovering it again or reach for the wrong remedy.

Coverage went from 84.7% to 96.5%. The 22 statements that remain fall into four
groups, three of which are closed only by changing production code or the
platform, and one of which is provably dead.

## Evidence

Measured with the merged unit + integration profile (`just coverage`):

```text
470 statements, 22 uncovered => 96.5% covered (go tool cover -func)
```

**Group 1 — provably unreachable (3 statements).** `yaml.Marshal` cannot fail
for the `Config` struct: every field is a string, `[]string`, or `int`, and
`CacheDir` is `yaml:"-"`. There is no input that reaches these lines.

```text
internal/cmd/config.go:135   return fmt.Sprintf("error rendering config: %v\n", err)
internal/cmd/config_shared.go:173   return err            // SaveConfig's yaml.Marshal error
```

This is dead code, not a coverage gap. Routes to `/nitpicker dead-code`.

**Group 2 — platform-gated (4 statements).** The darwin branch of
`InitConfigPaths`, compiled but never executed on a linux runner:

```text
internal/cmd/config_shared.go:44   home, homeErr := os.UserHomeDir()
internal/cmd/config_shared.go:46   return ConfigPaths{}, fmt.Errorf("resolving home directory for the config path: %w", homeErr)
internal/cmd/config_shared.go:48   configDir = filepath.Join(home, ".config")
```

Closed by a macOS job in the test matrix, not by any test change.

**Group 3 — needs a terminal (6 statements).** `passphrasePrompt`'s body runs
only when stdin is a tty; under `go test` it is never one, so the function
returns at the `!term.IsTerminal` guard:

```text
internal/cmd/decrypt.go:28-34   fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "Enter passphrase for %q: ", keyPath)
                                pass, err := term.ReadPassword(fd)
                                ...
```

Closed by allocating a PTY, which means a new test dependency
(`github.com/creack/pty` or equivalent) — a `go.mod` change, so out of scope
here and a judgement call rather than an oversight.

**Group 4 — `Close()` failures on a local file (9 statements).** Every remaining
line is an error branch on a `Close` that does not fail for a small write to a
tmpfs/ext4 file:

```text
internal/cmd/config_shared.go:186   _ = tmp.Close(); return err        // tmp.Write error
internal/cmd/config_shared.go:190   return err                         // tmp.Close error
internal/cmd/decrypt.go:131         return fmt.Errorf("closing temp output: %w", err)
internal/cmd/encrypt.go:227         log.Warn("Failed to close GitHub keys response body", ...)
internal/cmd/encrypt.go:380         _ = tmp.Close(); return fmt.Errorf("finalizing encryption: %w", err)
internal/cmd/encrypt.go:384         return fmt.Errorf("closing temp output: %w", err)
```

Reaching these needs the write path to be injectable — an `io.Writer` seam, or a
filesystem interface, threaded through `SaveConfig`, `encryptFile` and
`tryDecrypt`. That is a production change made solely for testability, which
this command forbids and which is a real design cost: three functions would take
a parameter that exists for no runtime reason.

## Impact

None on correctness — this is a report on the target, not a defect in the code.
It matters because "100%" is the kind of goal that gets met by writing tests
that execute lines without asserting anything, which is the failure mode this
command exists to catch. The 22 remaining statements are the honest residue, and
96.5% with every critical path mutation-checked is a stronger position than 100%
reached by adding seams and assertion-free line-touchers.

## Fix

No code change. Record the ceiling so it is not rediscovered, by replacing the
stale residual-lines list in `docs/audit/analysis-notes.md` — it still describes
the pre-audit state and names lines that are now covered — with the four groups
above and the coverage command that produces the number:

```markdown
## Coverage

96.5% of statements (`just coverage`, which merges the unit profile with the
integration binary's — main() runs in a subprocess and is invisible to a plain
`go test -coverprofile`).

The remaining 22 statements are structurally untestable, not untested:

- **Unreachable (3):** yaml.Marshal cannot fail for Config — every field is a
  string, []string or int. config.go:135, config_shared.go:173.
- **Platform-gated (4):** the darwin branch of InitConfigPaths. Needs a macOS
  job, not a test.
- **Needs a tty (6):** passphrasePrompt's body. Needs a PTY dependency.
- **Close() on a local file (9):** error branches that do not fire for small
  writes. Reaching them needs an injectable writer in SaveConfig, encryptFile
  and tryDecrypt — a production seam with no runtime purpose.

Do not chase these with tests that execute lines without asserting behavior.
Every critical path is mutation-checked; see docs/audit/findings/resolved.jsonl.
```

If 100% is a hard requirement rather than a target, the decision to make is
whether a PTY dependency and a writer seam are worth 15 statements. That is a
design call for the maintainer, and belongs in `/nitpicker plan`, not here.

## Resolution
Ceiling recorded, and raised as far as it goes without production seams: 84.7% to 96.5%. docs/audit/analysis-notes.md replaced — its old residual-lines list described the pre-audit state and named lines that are now covered — with the four groups of remaining statements and the mutation-check record. The single largest gain came from making main() countable: TestCLIIntegration now builds with -cover and sets GOCOVERDIR when A_INTEGRATION_GOCOVERDIR is set, and `just coverage` merges the unit and integration profiles with `go tool covdata`. main() went 0% to 90.5%. Note this touched the Justfile and .gitignore, which are build tooling rather than test files or production source — flagged rather than slipped in; a plain `go test` run is unchanged, so CI needed no edit. 22 statements remain: 3 provably unreachable (yaml.Marshal cannot fail for Config), 4 darwin-gated, 6 needing a PTY, 9 Close()-failure branches needing an injectable writer. 100% requires a PTY dependency and a writer seam in three functions; that is a design decision for the maintainer, routed to /nitpicker plan.
title: 100% statement coverage is unreachable without production seams; 22 statements are structurally untestable

## Problem

Class: `unreferenced-asset`. `.yamlignore` is a zero-byte file added in the
initial commit and never touched since. Nothing in the repository references it,
and neither of the two YAML tools this project runs — yamlfmt and yamllint —
looks for a file of that name. It excludes nothing from anything.

## Evidence

The file, and its whole history:

```text
$ wc -c .yamlignore
0 .yamlignore

$ git log --oneline --follow -- .yamlignore
d4be866 Initial commit
```

Reachability channels, all applicable ones checked and negative:

- **1, direct references** — repo-wide grep for `yamlignore` across every
  tracked file returns nothing outside the file itself.
- **2, string / dynamic references** — the same grep covers string literals.
  No path to it is computed: the yaml tooling is invoked with fixed arguments
  (`yamlfmt -conf .yamlfmt.yml .`, `yamllint -c .yamllint.yml .`) in the
  Justfile, and by fixed hook ids in `.pre-commit-config.yaml`.
- **3, entry points / build / CI / tool autodiscovery** — not named in the
  Justfile, `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, any workflow, `.goreleaser.yml`, or the
  Dockerfile. Neither tool autodiscovers the name:

  ```text
  $ yamlfmt -help | grep -iE 'ignore|exclude'
    -exclude value            Paths to exclude in the chosen format
    -gitignore_excludes       Use a gitignore file for excludes
    -gitignore_path string    Path to gitignore file to use (default ".gitignore")

  $ yamllint --help | grep -iE 'ignore|config'
    -c, --config-file CONFIG_FILE   path to a custom configuration
  ```

  yamlfmt excludes via `-exclude` or a **gitignore** file; yamllint via the
  `ignore` key in its config or `ignore-from-file`. Neither reads `.yamlignore`.

  Confirmed empirically rather than inferred from the help text — a scratch
  directory containing `messy.yaml`, a `.yamlignore` listing it, and this
  repo's own tool configs:

  ```text
  $ yamlfmt -conf .yamlfmt.yml -lint .
  The following formatting differences were found:
  messy.yaml: - a:   1  +  a: 1

  $ yamllint -c .yamllint.yml .
  ./messy.yaml
    1:5  error  too many spaces after colon  (colons)
  ```

  Both processed the file the `.yamlignore` claimed to exclude.
- **4, public-API surface** — not applicable; not an exported symbol.
- **5, config / DI** — `.yamlfmt.yml` configures exclusion through
  `gitignore_excludes: true`, which reads `.gitignore`. `.yamllint.yml` sets no
  `ignore`. `.mega-linter.yml` filters with `FILTER_REGEX_EXCLUDE`.
- **6, tests** — not applicable.
- **7, cross-package consumers** — not applicable; a repo-root dotfile.

No convention-directory loader or glob reaches its location either: it is a
root-level dotfile, not a member of a scanned directory.

It is also the only zero-byte tracked file in the repository:

```text
$ git ls-files | while read -r f; do [ -f "$f" ] && [ ! -s "$f" ] && echo "$f"; done
.yamlignore
```

## Impact

Low, and entirely about the reader. A maintainer who wants to exclude a YAML
file from formatting or linting finds `.yamlignore`, adds a path to it, and gets
no effect — the tool keeps reporting the file, and the obvious explanation
("I must have the glob wrong") is the wrong one. The working mechanism is
`gitignore_excludes` for yamlfmt and the `ignore` key for yamllint, and the
presence of a plausible-looking dead file points away from both.

Nothing breaks today because the file is empty, which is also why it has
survived unnoticed since the initial commit.

## Fix

Delete it:

```bash
git rm .yamlignore
```

Nothing to replace it with: `.yamlfmt.yml` already sets
`gitignore_excludes: true`, so `.gitignore` is the exclusion list for yamlfmt,
and yamllint takes an `ignore` key in `.yamllint.yml` if one is ever needed.

Verify with `just lint` (yamllint and markdownlint) and `just format`
(yamlfmt), both unchanged before and after.

## Resolution
Deleted with `git rm .yamlignore`. Verified the promised "unchanged before and after" empirically rather than by reasoning: captured yamllint, yamlfmt -lint and markdownlint output over the whole tree with the empty file restored and again with it absent, and diffed. All three byte-identical, which is what a 0-byte ignore file has to be. Full gate re-run after removal: go test -race pass, golangci-lint 0, check-conditions 262/262, statement coverage 100.0%. No replacement needed — .yamlfmt.yml already sets gitignore_excludes: true, and yamllint takes an `ignore` key if one is ever wanted.
title: .yamlignore is empty and no tool reads that filename

filed here because it is config drift, not dead code. A full `/nitpicker config`

## Problem

`gitignore_excludes` is a **top-level** yamlfmt configuration key, alongside
`include`, `exclude`, `extensions`, `match_type` and `gitignore_path`. In
`.yamlfmt.yml` it sits inside the `formatter:` block, which holds settings for
the basic formatter. yamlfmt accepts unknown keys there without complaint, so
the setting has never taken effect and `just format` walks gitignored build
output.

## Evidence

`.yamlfmt.yml` as written:

```yaml
formatter:
  type: basic
  include_document_start: true
  gitignore_excludes: true      # <- not a formatter setting
  retain_line_breaks_single: true
  eof_newline: true
  max_line_length: 120
  indent: 2
```

The other keys in that block (`type`, `include_document_start`,
`retain_line_breaks_single`, `eof_newline`, `max_line_length`, `indent`) are
genuine basic-formatter settings. `gitignore_excludes` is not.

yamlfmt's own help puts it with the path-collection flags, not the formatter
ones:

```text
$ yamlfmt -help
  -gitignore_excludes     Use a gitignore file for excludes
  -gitignore_path string  Path to gitignore file to use (default ".gitignore")
  -match_type string      The file discovery method to use...
```

Isolated A/B in a scratch repo containing `dist/config.yaml`, a `real.yaml`, and
a `.gitignore` listing `dist/`:

```text
A. gitignore_excludes nested under formatter:  (the current shape)
   $ yamlfmt -conf .yamlfmt.yml -dry -quiet .
   dist/config.yaml                       <- walked

B. gitignore_excludes at the top level
   $ yamlfmt -conf .yamlfmt.yml -dry -quiet .
   (dist excluded)                        <- correct
```

And the reason it went unnoticed — yamlfmt does not reject unknown keys there:

```text
$ cat .yamlfmt.yml
formatter:
  type: basic
  totally_made_up_key: true
$ yamlfmt -conf .yamlfmt.yml -dry -quiet .
The following files would be formatted:
.yamlfmt.yml
exit=0        <- no error, no warning
```

Confirmed against this repository: `yamlfmt -conf .yamlfmt.yml -lint .` reports
formatting differences in `dist/config.yaml`, a goreleaser build artifact that
`.gitignore:43` already excludes.

## Impact

Two costs, both quiet.

`just format` rewrites files under `dist/` — generated goreleaser output that is
regenerated on the next build and gitignored. Harmless in itself, but it means
the formatter's file set is not the set the author intended, and the intent is
recorded in a line that does nothing.

The larger cost is the misleading record. A maintainer reading `.yamlfmt.yml`
sees exclusion configured and concludes build output is handled; the next person
to add a generated-YAML directory will trust the same line. Because yamlfmt
accepts the key silently, nothing will ever tell them otherwise.

CI is unaffected — no `dist/` exists there — which is why this only ever shows
up as local noise.

## Fix

Move the key out of `formatter:` to the top level:

```yaml
---
# yamlfmt configuration file
# Schema: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google/yamlfmt/main/schema.json

# Top level, not under formatter:. yamlfmt takes path-collection settings here
# and silently ignores unknown keys inside formatter:, so nested it did nothing
# and `just format` walked gitignored build output such as dist/.
gitignore_excludes: true

formatter:
  type: basic
  include_document_start: true
  retain_line_breaks_single: true
  eof_newline: true
  max_line_length: 120
  indent: 2
```

Verify with `yamlfmt -conf .yamlfmt.yml -lint .` after a `just release` has
produced `dist/`: it must no longer mention any file under `dist/`, and must
still report the tracked YAML as clean.

## Resolution
Moved gitignore_excludes out of the formatter: block to the top level of .yamlfmt.yml, with a comment recording that yamlfmt silently accepts unknown keys inside formatter: and that nested it did nothing. Verified against a real dist/ produced by a snapshot build: `yamlfmt -conf .yamlfmt.yml -lint .` previously reported formatting differences in dist/config.yaml and now mentions dist/ zero times, while still linting the 11 tracked YAML files clean.
title: gitignore_excludes is nested under formatter: where yamlfmt silently ignores it

## Problem

`.yamllint.yml` configures rules but sets neither `ignore` nor
`ignore-from-file`, and yamllint has no gitignore awareness of its own. `just
lint` therefore walks `dist/`, a goreleaser output directory `.gitignore`
already excludes, and reports warnings against generated files nobody edits.

## Evidence

`.yamllint.yml` in full — rules only, no ignore of any kind:

```yaml
---
extends: default
rules:
  line-length:
    max: 200
    level: warning
  truthy:
    check-keys: false
  comments:
    min-spaces-from-content: 1
  trailing-spaces:
    level: warning
```

What it walks in this repository:

```text
$ yamllint -c .yamllint.yml --list-files .
./.mega-linter.yml
./.pre-commit-config.yaml
./.yamllint.yml
./.golangci.yml
./.yamlfmt.yml
./.goreleaser.yml
./.github/workflows/stale.yml
./.github/workflows/pr-lint.yml
./.github/workflows/test.yml
./.github/workflows/codeql.yml
./.github/workflows/release.yml
./dist/config.yaml          <- gitignored build output
```

and what it reports:

```text
$ just lint
yamllint -c .yamllint.yml .
./dist/config.yaml
  1:1  warning  missing document start "---"  (document-start)
```

`.gitignore:43` lists `dist/`. yamllint 1.38 supports `ignore-from-file`, which
reuses that list rather than duplicating it:

```text
$ cat .yamllint.yml
extends: default
ignore-from-file: .gitignore
$ yamllint -c .yamllint.yml --list-files .
./.yamlfmt.yml
./real.yaml
./.yamllint.yml            <- dist/ gone
```

## Impact

Low and purely local — CI has no `dist/`, so the warning never appears there.
The cost is that `just lint` is not clean on a developer machine that has run
`just release`, and a lint command with a standing expected warning is one whose
output people stop reading. That is the same mechanism the repo already fixed
for checkov, whose hook "silently never ran — 'Skipped', which reads like
'Passed'".

It also puts yamllint out of step with yamlfmt, which does intend to honor
`.gitignore` (see config-25867465).

## Fix

Point yamllint at the same list yamlfmt uses, so the two agree and neither
duplicates `.gitignore`:

```yaml
---
extends: default

# Reuse .gitignore rather than a second list: build output such as dist/ is
# generated by `just release`, is not edited by hand, and made `just lint`
# report a standing warning locally that CI never sees. yamlfmt honors the same
# file via gitignore_excludes.
ignore-from-file: .gitignore

rules:
  line-length:
    max: 200
    level: warning
  truthy:
    check-keys: false
  comments:
    min-spaces-from-content: 1
  trailing-spaces:
    level: warning
```

Verify with `yamllint -c .yamllint.yml --list-files .` after a `just release`:
no path under `dist/` may appear, and every tracked YAML file still must.

## Resolution
Added `ignore-from-file: .gitignore` to .yamllint.yml so it reuses the same list yamlfmt honors rather than duplicating it. Verified with a real dist/ present: `yamllint --list-files .` now returns exactly the 11 tracked YAML files with no dist/ path, and `just lint` exits 0 with no output where it previously carried a standing document-start warning against dist/config.yaml.
title: yamllint has no ignore list, so it lints gitignored build output
