Both packages are in scope of `./...` (`github.com/ivuorinen/a` and
`github.com/ivuorinen/a/internal/cmd`) and neither declares one. Nothing in the
tree is generated code: `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` is produced by
`scripts/gen-notices.sh` through `just notices`, and the findings `INDEX.md` by
`findings.py index` — neither is wired to `go generate`.

The sibling hook, `go mod tidy`, is not in question: it has a real effect and a
real purpose on a release build.

## Impact

Low. The cost is a release step that reads as load-bearing and is not: someone
debugging a release, or deciding whether generated code is current before
tagging, has to check whether `go generate` does anything here before they can
rule it out. It also runs unconditionally on a job holding `contents: write`,
which is a stage worth keeping to what is actually needed.

There is a defensive reading — if a `//go:generate` is added later, the release
would pick it up. That is speculative: nothing indicates code generation is
planned, and if it were added, `just notices`-style wiring would be the local
precedent rather than this hook.

## Fix

Drop the line:

```yaml
before:
  hooks:
    - go mod tidy
```

If code generation is ever introduced, add the hook back together with the
directive that needs it, so the two arrive as one reviewable change.

Verify with `goreleaser check` and a `just release` snapshot build, both of
which must behave exactly as before.

## Resolution
Removed `go generate ./...` from .goreleaser.yml's before.hooks, leaving `go mod tidy`. Verified: `goreleaser check` validates, and a snapshot build logs `running hook=go mod tidy` with no generate step and succeeds. If code generation is ever added, the hook should return alongside the //go:generate directive that needs it, as one reviewable change.
title: The release runs `go generate ./...` and the repo has no go:generate directives

body:
Surfaced by the `dead-code` run and routed here as dead flexibility. A full
`/nitpicker complexity` lens has not been run.

## Problem

`.mega-linter.yml` sets both `ENABLE_LINTERS` and `DISABLE_LINTERS`.
`ENABLE_LINTERS` is an allow-list: when present, only the linters it names run.
`REPOSITORY_DEVSKIM` is not among them, so it never runs, and the
`DISABLE_LINTERS` entry removes it from a set it was never in.

## Evidence

`.mega-linter.yml`, the two keys as written:

```yaml
DISABLE_LINTERS:
  - REPOSITORY_DEVSKIM
ENABLE_LINTERS:
  - YAML_YAMLLINT
  - MARKDOWN_MARKDOWNLINT
  - YAML_PRETTIER
  - JSON_PRETTIER
```

The file's own comment states the allow-list semantics, three lines above:

```yaml
# ENABLE_LINTERS below is an allow-list -- deleting it does not disable CI
# linting, it unleashes MegaLinter's full default linter set (GO_GOLANGCI_LINT
# and GO_REVIVE included) on every PR.
```

If deleting `ENABLE_LINTERS` would unleash the full default set, then while it
is present only those four linters run — and disabling a fifth that is already
excluded by construction changes nothing.

This is the same shape as the 19-entry `disable:` block removed from
`.golangci.yml` earlier in this session (audit-59990286), where
`golangci-lint linters` printed an empty "Disabled by your configuration"
section against nineteen entries that read as deliberate exclusions.

## Impact

Low, and the same reader cost as its `.golangci.yml` counterpart. Two lines that
look like a considered security-linter exclusion are inert. Someone auditing
what MegaLinter enforces has to work out the precedence between the two keys
before they can conclude the entry means nothing; someone who instead trusts it
learns the wrong rule and may add more entries to a list that does not act.

There is a defensive reading — if `ENABLE_LINTERS` were ever removed, the
disable would start mattering. That is exactly the "dead flexibility" this
routes as: it protects against an edit the file's own comment warns against
making.

## Fix

Delete the two lines:

```yaml
APPLY_FIXES: all
SHOW_ELAPSED_TIME: false
...
ENABLE_LINTERS:
  - YAML_YAMLLINT
  - MARKDOWN_MARKDOWNLINT
  - YAML_PRETTIER
  - JSON_PRETTIER
```

If DevSkim specifically must stay off even should the allow-list be removed,
that intent belongs in the `ENABLE_LINTERS` comment, where a reader is already
being told the list is load-bearing — not in a key that does nothing while the
list exists.

Verify with `yamllint -c .yamllint.yml .mega-linter.yml`. Behavior cannot change:
the linter set is determined by `ENABLE_LINTERS`, which is untouched.

## Resolution
Deleted the two DISABLE_LINTERS lines from .mega-linter.yml. ENABLE_LINTERS is untouched and remains the allow-list that determines the linter set, so behavior cannot change. Verified the file still lints clean. Same class as audit-59990286, the no-op disable block removed from .golangci.yml earlier in this session.
title: DISABLE_LINTERS disables a linter the ENABLE_LINTERS allow-list never enables

body:
## Problem

Class: `config-drift` — an in-code source of truth disagreeing with the actual
config surface. The docstring on `defaultCacheTTLMinutes` states that the
constant matches the default of a `--cache-ttl` flag. The CLI has no such flag,
and never has. A maintainer reading the constant is told there are two places
this value is declared, and looks for a second one that is not there.

## Evidence

internal/cmd/config_shared.go:15-17:

```go
// defaultCacheTTLMinutes is the GitHub-key cache lifetime written to a freshly
// bootstrapped config. It matches the --cache-ttl flag default.
const defaultCacheTTLMinutes = 120
```

Every flag the CLI actually registers:

```text
./internal/cmd/encrypt.go:139  input      -i
./internal/cmd/encrypt.go:140  output     -o
./internal/cmd/encrypt.go:141  recipient  -r
./internal/cmd/encrypt.go:142  github-user
./internal/cmd/encrypt.go:143  force      -f
./internal/cmd/decrypt.go:243  input      -i
./internal/cmd/decrypt.go:244  output     -o
./internal/cmd/decrypt.go:245  ssh-key
./internal/cmd/decrypt.go:246  force      -f
./a.go:177                     verbose    -v
```

Confirmed against the built binary rather than the source alone:

```text
$ for c in "" encrypt decrypt config completion; do a $c --help | grep -oE '\-\-[a-z-]+'; done | sort -u
--force --github-user --help --input --output --recipient --ssh-key --verbose --version
```

The string `cache-ttl` appears in exactly one place in the repository — the
docstring itself (plus its copy inside the generated `coverage.html`):

```text
$ grep -rn 'cache-ttl' . --exclude-dir=.git --exclude-dir=dist
internal/cmd/config_shared.go:16:// bootstrapped config. It matches the --cache-ttl flag default.
```

The TTL is settable only through the config file, via
`a config set cache_ttl_minutes <n>`.

## Impact

The repo's documentation rule is that a docstring records what the reader cannot
recover from the code, and this one records something that contradicts it. Two
concrete costs:

A maintainer changing the default has been told to keep a flag default in sync
and will go looking for it; finding nothing, they either waste the search or
conclude the flag was lost in a refactor and consider re-adding it.

It also misstates the config surface. The constant is the *only* declaration of
this default — the point worth recording is that it is single-sourced and that
`a config rem cache_ttl_minutes` restores it, which is what the README now says.
The docstring claims the opposite shape.

`.golangci.yml`'s `godox` linter catches TODO/FIXME drift but nothing catches a
docstring naming a flag that does not exist, so this survived every check.

## Fix

Replace the false sentence with what is actually true of the constant:

```go
// defaultCacheTTLMinutes is the GitHub-key cache lifetime written to a freshly
// bootstrapped config, and the value `a config rem cache_ttl_minutes` restores.
// There is no flag for it: the TTL is config-file only, so this constant is its
// single declaration.
const defaultCacheTTLMinutes = 120
```

Verify with `grep -rn 'cache-ttl' . --exclude-dir=.git --exclude-dir=dist`,
which must return nothing outside generated artifacts, and confirm the README's
`cache_ttl_minutes` row still states `120` as the default.

## Resolution
Replaced the false sentence on defaultCacheTTLMinutes. The docstring now says the constant is the value `a config rem cache_ttl_minutes` restores, that there is no flag for it, and that it is therefore the single declaration of the default. Verified: `grep -rn 'cache-ttl'` over the tree now returns nothing outside generated artifacts, and the README's cache_ttl_minutes row still states 120.
title: defaultCacheTTLMinutes is documented as matching a --cache-ttl flag that does not exist

body:
## Problem

Class: `missing-validation`. `cache_ttl_minutes` is read from the config file
as an `int` and converted to a duration with `time.Duration(ttlMinutes) *
time.Minute`. Nothing bounds it. `time.Duration` is int64 nanoseconds, so any
value above 153,722,867 overflows, and the resulting duration is not merely
wrong — it is non-monotonic. A larger number can produce a shorter TTL, a
negative one, or a plausible-looking long one.

## Evidence

The read and the conversion — internal/cmd/encrypt.go:265-270:

```go
func readKeyCache(cachePath string, ttlMinutes int) ([]string, bool) {
    info, err := os.Stat(cachePath)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, false
    }
    if time.Since(info.ModTime()) > time.Duration(ttlMinutes)*time.Minute {
        return nil, false
    }
```

Neither of the two paths that set the value bounds it. `setConfigKey`
(internal/cmd/config.go:118-123) accepts anything `strconv.Atoi` parses, and a
value written straight into `config.yaml` is accepted by `yaml.Unmarshal` as
long as it is an integer.

Measured, not reasoned:

```text
cache_ttl_minutes=120         -> 2h0m0s                     negative=false
cache_ttl_minutes=153722867   -> 2562047h47m0s              negative=false
cache_ttl_minutes=153722868   -> -2562047h46m33.709551616s  negative=true
cache_ttl_minutes=200000000   -> -1790762h14m33.709551616s  negative=true
cache_ttl_minutes=307445734   -> -33.709551616s             negative=true
cache_ttl_minutes=999999999   -> 1294379h55m18.871345152s   negative=false
```

Failing scenario: a user who wants the GitHub key cache to effectively never
expire sets

```yaml
cache_ttl_minutes: 200000000
```

The duration wraps negative, `time.Since(...) > negative` is true for every
cache file, `readKeyCache` reports a miss every time, and every `a encrypt`
against a GitHub user makes a fresh network request. The cache is silently off
— the opposite of what was asked for, with no error and nothing in the log.

The non-monotonicity is what makes it hard to diagnose: `999999999` happens to
land on a positive ~147-year duration and works, while the smaller `200000000`
does not. A user bisecting the value gets inconsistent results.

The README documents that "zero or negative disables caching entirely", so the
negative case is understood behavior — but the operator never typed a negative
number, and nothing tells them their positive one became one.

## Impact

Low. It is self-inflicted, needs an absurd value, and the failure direction is
safe: the cache stops being used, so `a` fetches fresh keys rather than serving
stale ones. No security, correctness, or data consequence.

What earns the finding is that it is silent and misleading. The tool accepts the
value, `a config show` echoes it back unchanged, and the behavior contradicts
both the value and the documentation, with no way to tell from the outside.

## Fix

Reject out-of-range values where they are set, using the project's existing
`strconv` path — no new dependency, and the message names the ceiling:

```go
// internal/cmd/config.go, in setConfigKey's cache_ttl_minutes case
n, err := strconv.Atoi(value)
if err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("cache_ttl_minutes must be an integer: %w", err)
}
// time.Duration is int64 nanoseconds, so minutes above this overflow and wrap
// -- a larger number can yield a shorter or negative TTL, silently disabling
// the cache the operator was trying to extend.
if n > maxCacheTTLMinutes {
    return fmt.Errorf("cache_ttl_minutes must be at most %d (about 292 years); "+
        "larger values overflow the duration and disable caching", maxCacheTTLMinutes)
}
cfg.CacheTTLMinutes = n
```

with, in config_shared.go beside the existing default:

```go
// maxCacheTTLMinutes is the largest TTL that survives conversion to a
// time.Duration: math.MaxInt64 nanoseconds / time.Minute.
const maxCacheTTLMinutes = int(math.MaxInt64 / int64(time.Minute))
```

That covers `a config set`. A value written directly into `config.yaml` bypasses
`setConfigKey`, so clamp at the point of use as well, which is the one line that
actually matters:

```go
// internal/cmd/encrypt.go, readKeyCache
ttl := time.Duration(min(ttlMinutes, maxCacheTTLMinutes)) * time.Minute
if time.Since(info.ModTime()) > ttl {
    return nil, false
}
```

Verify with a table test over the six values measured above, asserting the
resulting TTL is positive and monotonic in the input.

## Resolution
Added maxCacheTTLMinutes = int(math.MaxInt64 / int64(time.Minute)) in config_shared.go — derived rather than written out so it cannot drift — and used it in two places: setConfigKey rejects anything larger with a message naming the ceiling, and readKeyCache clamps with min() because a value written straight into config.yaml never passes through setConfigKey. A negative TTL still passes through unclamped, preserving the documented "zero or negative disables caching". Verified: the constant is 153722867 and fits int32, so linux/386 and linux/arm still build; clamping holds 153722868, 200000000 and 999999999 all at ~292 years instead of wrapping. Two tests added — TestConfig_SetCacheTTLRejectsOverflow covers both sides of the new branch (boundary accepted, boundary+1 refused and not stored) and TestReadKeyCache_OverflowingTTLStillHits covers the clamp. Condition coverage went 262/262 to 264/264, statement coverage still 100.0%.
title: cache_ttl_minutes has no range check, so a large value overflows into a negative TTL
